Name: acquisition_language_anchor
Title: Anchored to Where It Was Learned: A Per-Fact Acquisition-Language Anchor That Hides Cross-Lingual Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: Each fact carries a per-fact 'acquisition-language anchor' - the language in which the model predominantly encountered it during training, estimated by a Wikipedia-coverage proxy and validated against true corpus counts on an open-data model - and cross-lingual recall is routed through that anchor's representation regardless of the query language. The falsifiable prediction that distinguishes this from the fixed-English-hub account, in one sentence: for a non-English-anchored fact the model will succeed in the anchor language and fail in English (a reverse-direction failure the English-hub account forbids). Many cross-lingual failures are anchor-override failures: when the query language differs from the fact's anchor the model fails even though the fact is stored, and the failure direction is predicted by anchor-vs-query mismatch rather than by a fixed English hub. We hypothesize (1) the anchor is decodable from intermediate activations, distinct from the query-language signal; (2) which query directions fail is predicted by anchor-vs-query mismatch above a fixed-English-hub baseline AND above a corpus-frequency-only baseline; and (3) suppressing anchor-language routing (or steering the language-transition earlier toward the query language) recovers the stored fact without editing it. The explicit null we test against is that the apparent anchor is nothing but language prevalence / corpus frequency / English bias.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic work shows multilingual LLMs recall facts through an English-centric pipeline then translate to the target language (Paths Not Taken 2025; Lost in Multilinguality 2025), and that cross-lingual inconsistency has a middle/final-layer bottleneck (Are Knowledge and Reference Cross-Lingually Consistent 2025). Beyond the Rosetta Stone (2025) shows unified-vs-separate representations form early in training and drive transfer. Language Models' Factuality Depends on the Language of Inquiry (2025) and ECLeKTic (2025) benchmark the phenomenon that a fact known in one language fails in another. Our novelty is a mixture we make explicit: the MECHANISM (per-fact anchor routing that can be non-English), the FINDING (reverse-direction failures), and the MEASUREMENT (a proxy-validated per-fact anchor label). All prior accounts privilege a fixed English hub and treat failure as insufficient engagement of the English mechanism or bad translation; none posit a per-fact, data-driven acquisition-language anchor, none show the direction of failure is predicted by anchor-vs-query mismatch better than a fixed-English-hub OR a corpus-frequency model, and none demonstrate recovery by suppressing anchor-language routing. This transfers our temporal_anchor_override logic from time to language: a query-independent default (the acquisition language) overrides the query-specified frame. Practitioner takeaway if supported: multilingual reliability requires anchor-aware evaluation and training-mix balancing, not just 'does the model know it?'.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs often 'know' a fact in one language yet fail to produce it in another - a user-visible reliability gap for anyone querying an assistant outside English. The prevailing mechanistic account routes all recall through an English-centric hub and blames failure on weak English engagement or faulty back-translation. We propose a per-fact account: each fact has an acquisition-language anchor - the language in which the model predominantly encountered it during training - and cross-lingual recall is routed through that anchor's representation regardless of query language. We define the anchor operationally and non-circularly (a Wikipedia-coverage proxy, validated against true training-corpus language counts on the open-data model OLMo) and test it against an explicit null that the anchor is merely corpus frequency or English bias. Under this view, whether a given query language succeeds is governed by anchor-vs-query mismatch, and failures are anchor-override failures: the fact is stored (recoverable in the anchor language) but the query language cannot access it. We test three claims across a controlled multilingual fact set with anchors that are frequently non-English. (1) Localization: a linear probe recovers a per-fact anchor-language signal from intermediate activations, separable (via residualization) from the query-language signal. (2) Predictiveness: anchor-vs-query mismatch predicts which query directions fail, with higher AUROC than both a fixed-English-hub and a frequency-only baseline (controlling for answer frequency, script similarity, and fact popularity), and non-English-anchored facts show reverse-direction failures - fail in English, succeed in the anchor. (3) Causal recovery: suppressing anchor-language routing, or steering the transition earlier toward the query language, recovers stored facts with higher specificity and less collateral damage than fact editing or generic English-pivot prompting. The practical implication is concrete: anchor-aware probing and data balancing, and inference-time routing interventions, for multilingual deployments. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H2 — Anchor-labeled dataset and reverse-direction prevalence): Tests the premise of H2, that non-English-anchored facts fail in the reverse direction (recalled in the anchor, failed in English), which a fixed-English-hub account forbids. Data: constructed. Source (a) country/culture-anchored entities (people, places, dishes) whose Wikipedia coverage is dominant in a specific non-English language, using per-language article length/presence as anchor proxy following ECLeKTic (existing, ~2.5k items); source (b) Language-Specific-Knowledge items (existing). We assemble 3,000 facts, each with semantically-equivalent queries in 6 languages (spanning Latin/Cyrillic/CJK/Arabic scripts) plus verified translations, restricted to single-token-first answers (report coverage; expect ~60% retained). 3,000 x 6 = 18,000 queries is enough for >=300 facts per anchor language and fits an academic inference budget. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen (bf16), greedy. Systems compared: observed best-recall language per fact vs the fixed-English-hub null (English strongest for all). Decisive metric (before data): fraction of non-English-anchored facts whose best-recall language is non-English AND English fails. Convincing = >=25% of non-English-anchored facts show this reverse pattern, CI excluding a 5% chance rate. Negative = <=5% (English hub holds; the anchor premise fails). Indecision band 5-25%: report weak anchoring, insufficient to displace the English-hub account.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Anchor-vs-query mismatch predicts which query directions fail): Tests H2's predictiveness claim against the fixed-English-hub baseline. Data: all (fact, query-language) pairs from Exp 1 (~18,000), split 80/20 by fact. Model: same three frozen models; a logistic regression over pair features, trained seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: predictor A = per-fact anchor-vs-query mismatch; baseline B = fixed-English-hub (mismatch := query != English); baseline C = per-language fact-frequency only; all controlling for answer frequency and script similarity. Decisive metric (before data), first: held-out AUROC of A minus AUROC of B for predicting recall failure. Convincing = A beats B by >=0.05 AUROC with paired bootstrap CI excluding 0, and A's absolute AUROC >=0.70. Negative = A <= B (per-fact anchor adds nothing over an English hub; H2 fails). Indecision band 0.00-0.05 AUROC gain: report the anchor as a marginal refinement of the English-hub model, not a replacement.

Experiment 3 (H1 — Anchor-signal localization): Tests H1, that a per-fact anchor language is decodable from intermediate activations, distinct from the query-language signal. Data: activations for the Exp 1 queries; probe train/test split 80/20 by fact. Model: same three frozen models; two linear probes per layer on the subject-token and last-token residual stream -- one decoding the per-fact anchor label, one decoding the query language -- L2-regularized, seeds {0,1,2}, layer by CV. Systems compared: anchor probe vs query-language probe vs label-shuffle control (chance); anchor probe residualized on the query-language signal to test non-redundancy. Decisive metric (before data): residual per-fact anchor AUROC after removing query-language information, best layer, held-out. Convincing = residual AUROC >=0.70 and the resolution layer overlaps the known language-transition band. Negative = <=0.55 (anchor not separable from query language; H1 fails). Indecision band 0.55-0.70: report an entangled, graded anchor signal. Shuffle control must sit at ~0.50.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Storage verification and causal recovery of hidden facts): Tests H3, that suppressing anchor-language routing (or steering the transition earlier toward the query language) recovers a stored fact without editing it. Data: anchor-override failures = (fact, query-language) pairs that fail in the query language but succeed in the anchor language AND whose answer is decodable by a content probe during the failing run (verified-stored; report coverage; exclude facts with answer tokens shared across languages). Target 1,200 verified-override pairs. Model: same three frozen models; interventions are activation edits at the identified transition layers (from Exp 3), no weight training; dose alpha in {0,0.5,1,2,4}. Systems compared, matched norm: (a) patch anchor-language routing from a successful anchor run; (b) suppress the anchor-language direction; (c) steer the transition earlier toward the query language; (d) reverse control injecting the anchor direction; plus random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data): per-pair recovery rate (correct answer now emitted IN the query language) over random control. Convincing = >=30pp gain over random at a dose keeping per-language perplexity within 5%. Negative = <=5pp (routing suppression does not recover; H3 fails). Indecision band 5-30pp: partial causal support; reverse control must raise override by >=10pp.

Experiment 5 (H3 — Recovery specificity and collateral cost): Tests that H3's recovery is specific. Data: Exp 4 held-out override pairs; 1,000 (fact, query-language) pairs already recalled correctly in the query language; 200 unrelated facts. Model: same three frozen, best intervention/dose from Exp 4. Systems compared: our intervention vs the Paths-Not-Taken translation/recall vectors (existing), English-pivot prompting ('answer in English then translate'), ROME editing (existing, expected null since the fact is stored), and random-direction control. Decisive metric (before data), first: recovery rate MINUS accuracy drop on already-correct query-language pairs (recovered-per-unit-collateral). Convincing = recovery >=25pp while already-correct accuracy drops <=3pp, unrelated-fact accuracy drops <=2pp, per-language perplexity rises <=5%. Negative = collateral drop >=10pp or no net recovery. Indecision band 3-10pp already-correct drop: utility capped; report the trade-off. ROME expected <=5pp recovery, confirming the fact is hidden, not absent.

Experiment 6 (H3 — Cross-relation and cross-language-pair transfer): Tests whether a single anchor-suppression/early-transition vector generalizes rather than being pair-specific. Data: vector fit on a subset of relations/language pairs (from Exp 4) applied unchanged to held-out relations and held-out language pairs (800 override pairs). Model: all three frozen models. Systems compared: transferred vector vs in-domain-refit vector vs random-direction. Decisive metric (before data): transferred recovery rate as a fraction of in-domain-refit recovery. Convincing = >=60% of in-domain on >=2 models. Negative = <=20% (anchoring is pair-specific; practical generality fails). Indecision band 20-60%: partial transfer. Also report Spearman rho between model scale and override rate across the three models (rho <=-0.3 = suggestive that larger models anchor less, N=3 caveat).

Experiment 7 (H1 — Anchor-proxy validation and source analysis on an open-data model): Tests that the Wikipedia-coverage anchor proxy used throughout tracks true training-corpus language and thereby underpins the H1 anchor construct. Data: OLMo-7B (existing open-data model whose training-corpus language distribution is inspectable); for 1,000 facts compute the true per-fact dominant training language from corpus counts and the Wikipedia-coverage proxy. Model: OLMo-7B frozen; reuse the Exp 1-3 pipeline. Systems compared: proxy-derived anchor vs corpus-derived anchor. Decisive metric (before data): agreement (Cohen's kappa) between proxy anchor and corpus anchor, and whether corpus-derived mismatch predicts failure at least as well as proxy-derived mismatch (AUROC). Convincing = kappa >=0.5 and corpus-mismatch AUROC within 0.03 of proxy-mismatch AUROC. Negative = kappa <=0.2 (proxy invalid; all anchor labels suspect, weakening H1/H2 interpretation). Indecision band kappa 0.2-0.5: treat the anchor as approximate and flag proxy limits, as the Risk section already notes.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The acquisition-language anchor is estimated via a Wikipedia-coverage proxy, which may be inaccurate for closed models; we validate the proxy on an open-data model (OLMo) and report proxy limitations, treating the anchor as approximate.

The anchor account may collapse to the fixed-English-hub account if most facts are in fact English-anchored; the deliberate inclusion of strongly non-English-anchored facts (Exp 1-2) and the AUROC comparison (Exp 3) are the decisive tests, and a partial improvement over the English-hub baseline is still informative.
Anchor-language and query-language signals may be entangled; the causal patching/steering tests (Exp 6), not probe AUROC alone, are decisive, and graded results remain informative.

Verifying a fact is 'stored' via anchor-language recall risks overestimation from surface entity-token leakage (shared names); we exclude facts with shared answer tokens across languages and use conservative content-probe thresholds, reporting coverage.

Interventions could degrade fluency in the query language or over-recover (force English-derived answers awkwardly); per-language specificity and perplexity controls are central and utility may be capped.
A single transferable intervention vector may not exist if anchoring is language-pair-specific, limiting practical generality though still scientifically informative.
Multi-token answers and cross-script tokenization complicate readout; primary analysis restricts to single-token-first answers with reported coverage.
Findings on 7-9B models may not transfer to frontier-scale models beyond an academic budget.
